$comment: WHO USES @broberg/sso — the list I notify on every release.
Christian's standing order, 2026-09-20: every release of this package is
announced to broberg-id AND every known consumer, at PUBLISH time — not
when somebody is about to upgrade. The day it was given, 0.2.1 had spent
an hour on npm rejecting every token the real Broberg ID issues.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS RATHER THAN A LOOKUP. Discovery is the right place to
ask 'who uses X', and it was MEASURED EMPTY for this package the same day:
131 enrolment rows, 0 mentioning sso. A rule whose data source is empty is
not a rule, it is a reminder — so the list lives here, in the repo that
publishes the package, and the release gate reads it out loud.
EVERY ENTRY CARRIES ITS EVIDENCE. `version` is what was MEASURED in their
tree, `as_of` is when, and `source` is how. An entry whose as_of is old is
visibly old rather than quietly wrong — that is the whole difference
between a register and a note.
Adding one: measure first, then write the row. Never write what a session
says it is planning to run.

A ROW NAMES A REPO; A DEPENDENCY LIVES IN AN APP. broberg-id, 2026-09-22: our row said version 0.1.0 for repo broberg-ai/broberg-id, and BID ITSELF has zero occurrences of the package in its package.json — it is the ISSUER. So the number did not merely go stale, the row described something that does not exist. `installs` now carries one entry per app that actually depends on the package, because a repo-shaped row cannot hold two apps on two pins.

DO NOT ASK 'HOW MANY TIMES IS THE SYMBOL MENTIONED' — THAT COUNT ANSWERS BACKWARDS. Measured by helpdesk, 2026-09-22, against a grep I had handed them: 10 hits in their repo, every one of them a plan-doc ABOUT the breaking change plus a guard test that FORBIDS the symbol's use. Real call-sites: zero. The more carefully a repo has handled a breaking change, the more often it names the thing — so a repo with 10 hits and a repo with 0 can be the one that closed it completely and the one that never thought about it. Ask whether a CALL PATH reads it, never how many lines contain it.
A version here is what was MEASURED in their tree, never what they said they would run.

consumers.role: issuer — and NOT a consumer in its own service
consumers.uses: BID ITSELF DOES NOT DEPEND ON @broberg/sso — zero occurrences in its package.json (their measurement, re-confirmed 2026-09-22). It is the issuer. The dependency lives only in their two example apps, and they publish the public integration guide at id.broberg.ai/docs.md, which is what makes a wrong version number there expensive
consumers.source: their own measurement in node_modules (pin AND installed) after taking 0.3.0 on Christian's order. They proved the three codes against the REAL adapter rather than reading them in our report, including that the cookie is cleared in the same response — a claim that had been FALSE in their own guide for an hour that morning (their text promised the clearing; their code only did it when the login SUCCEEDED, fixed in 058ef04)
consumers.notify: always, first — a release that changes verification changes their own service's story
consumers.guide_floor: ^0.2.3 in docs/BRUG-BID.md + llms.txt — deliberately the version where the two properties the text describes actually landed, not the newest. The examples sit above the floor; a reader following ^0.2.3 gets latest in practice

consumers.uses: core only (createSsoClient), NOT the Hono adapter — their session is keyed on their own userId, so the adapter's own cookie would be a second opinion about who is logged in. NO FEDERATED LOGOUT (their measurement, 2026-09-22): POST /auth/logout clears only their own session cookie and never redirects to BID's end-session, so there is no foreign confirmation page to get past and no id_token_hint to be missing. The consequence is real and theirs: logging out of HelpDesk leaves the BID session alive. It means README's "store the ID token" does not apply to every core consumer — not storing it is the OTHER valid shape
consumers.source: their own measurement after taking 0.3.0 on Christian's order: apps/core/package.json pins "0.3.0" exact, CI green on 8f8c966, and all five core symbols unchanged in 0.3.0's .d.ts. Zero real uses of the three callback error codes, zero imports of the Hono adapter — counted AFTER excluding their own plan-doc and the guard test that forbids the use
consumers.notify: always — BID's app #1, and the package is the only door into their product
consumers.pin_style: EXACT on purpose — prod-auth dependency, per the fleet exact-pin rule. So the 0.x caret trap (^0.1.0 follows 0.1.x only) does NOT explain why they are behind; a deliberate pin does. Two very different reasons that look identical from the registry
consumers.breaking_check: 0.3.0's split of /callback's error code is NOT breaking for them, measured rather than assumed — and they made the answer falsifiable instead of leaving it as a dated claim: sso-overflade.guard.test.ts scans apps/ + tests/ and goes red if any of the three codes is used or /hono is imported. Their trap, worth copying: a comment in bid.ts NAMES the adapter to explain why they do not use it, so without stripping comments first the guard reddens on the very file it protects — and gets switched off the same day

notify_beyond_this_file: MEASURED BY broberg-id 2026-09-20, the whole client table at BID:
One real consumer, and it IS a cc session — so today my list and theirs
are the same set, and 'tell broberg-id, they tell the rest' costs nothing.
THAT ASSUMPTION DIES AT CUSTOMER TWO, and they said so rather than letting
it be discovered: FDAA gets its OWN tenant on its own domain, i.e. a
separate BID deployment with a client table neither they nor I can read
from here. There is no mechanism today for reaching a client that is not a
cc session, and none that spans tenants. Theirs to build; ours to stop
assuming. When a consumer appears that is not a session, this file cannot
answer the question it exists for.
